p: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires,—
(a) “Committee” means a Committee constituted under article 243S;
(b) “district” means a district in a State;

(c) “Metropolitan area” means an area having a population of ten lakhs or more, comprised in one or more districts and consisting of two or more Municipalities or Panchayats or other contiguous areas, specified by the Governor by public notification to be a Metropolitan area for the purposes of this Part;
(d) “Municipal area” means the territorial area of a Municipality as is notified by the Governor;
(e) “Municipality” means an institution of self-government constituted under article 243Q;
(f) “Panchayat” means a Panchayat constituted under article 243B;
(g) “population” means the population as ascertained at the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published.
243P.s: Defines key terms for the Municipalities Part, such as a Metropolitan area: an area of ten lakhs or more people, covering one or more districts and two or more Municipalities or Panchayats, notified by the Governor. Population means the count at the last published census.

p: (1) There shall be constituted in every State,—
(a) a Nagar Panchayat (by whatever name called) for a transitional area, that is to say, an area in transition from a rural area to an urban area;
(b) a Municipal Council for a smaller urban area; and
(c) a Municipal Corporation for a larger urban area,
in accordance with the provisions of this Part:

Provided that a Municipality under this clause may not be constituted in such urban area or part thereof as the Governor may, having regard to the size of the area and the municipal services being provided or proposed to be provided by an industrial establishment in that area and such other factors as he may deem fit, by public notification, specify to be an industrial township.

(2) In this article, “a transitional area”, “a smaller urban area” or “a larger urban area” means such area as the Governor may, having regard to the population of the area, the density of the population therein, the revenue generated for local administration, the percentage of employment in non-agricultural activities, the economic importance or such other factors as he may deem fit, specify by public notification for the purposes of this Part.
243Q.s: Every State must set up a Nagar Panchayat for an area changing from rural to urban, a Municipal Council for a smaller urban area, and a Municipal Corporation for a larger urban area. The Governor classifies areas by population, density, revenue, non-agricultural jobs and similar factors, and can exempt industrial townships.

p: (1) Save as provided in clause (2), all the seats in a Municipality shall be filled by persons chosen by direct election from the territorial constituencies in the Municipal area and for this purpose each Municipal area shall be divided into territorial constituencies to be known as wards.
(2) The Legislature of a State may, by law, provide—
(a) for the representation in a Municipality of—
(i) persons having special knowledge or experience in Municipal administration;
(ii) the members of the House of the People and the members of the Legislative Assembly of the State representing constituencies which comprise wholly or partly the Municipal area;
(iii) the members of the Council of States and the members of the Legislative Council of the State registered as electors within the Municipal area;
(iv) the Chairpersons of the Committees constituted under clause (5) of article 243S:
Provided that the persons referred to in paragraph (i) shall not have the right to vote in the meetings of the Municipality;
(b) the manner of election of the Chairperson of a Municipality.
243R.s: Municipality seats are filled by direct election from wards. The State Legislature can also, by law, add experts in municipal administration (who cannot vote), Lok Sabha and Assembly members whose constituencies cover the area, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council members registered there, and chairpersons of the other committees set up under Article 243S(5), and decide how the Chairperson is elected.

p: (1) There shall be constituted Wards Committees, consisting of one or more wards, within the territorial area of a Municipality having a population of three lakhs or more.
(2) The Legislature of a State may, by law, make provision with respect to—
(a) the composition and the territorial area of a Wards Committee;
(b) the manner in which the seats in a Wards Committee shall be filled.
(3) A member of a Municipality representing a ward within the territorial area of the Wards Committee shall be a member of that Committee.
(4) Where a Wards Committee consists of—
(a) one ward, the member representing that ward in the Municipality; or
(b) two or more wards, one of the members representing such wards in the Municipality elected by the members of the Wards Committee,
shall be the Chairperson of that Committee.
(5) Nothing in this article shall be deemed to prevent the Legislature of a State from making any provision for the constitution of Committees in addition to the Wards Committees.
243S.s: Every Municipality with a population of three lakhs or more must have Wards Committees of one or more wards, which include the Municipality's members for those wards. The ward member chairs it or, for several wards, one of those ward members elected by the Committee does, and States decide the rest and can create other committees.

p: (1) Seats shall be reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in every Municipality and the number of seats so reserved shall bear, as nearly as may be, the same proportion to the total number of seats to be filled by direct election in that Municipality as the population of the Scheduled Castes in the Municipal area or of the Scheduled Tribes in the Municipal area bears to the total population of that area and such seats may be allotted by rotation to different constituencies in a Municipality.
(2) Not less than one-third of the total number of seats reserved under clause (1) shall be reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes or, as the case may be, the Scheduled Tribes.

(3) Not less than one-third (including the number of seats reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes) of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election in every Municipality shall be reserved for women and such seats may be allotted by rotation to different constituencies in a Municipality.
(4) The offices of Chairpersons in the Municipalities shall be reserved for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes and women in such manner as the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide.

(5) The reservation of seats under clauses (1) and (2) and the reservation of offices of Chairpersons (other than the reservation for women) under clause (4) shall cease to have effect on the expiration of the period specified in article 334.

(6) Nothing in this Part shall prevent the Legislature of a State from making any provision for reservation of seats in any Municipality or offices of Chairpersons in the Municipalities in favour of backward class of citizens.
243T.s: Municipality seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their local population, with at least one-third of those for SC or ST women, and at least one-third of all directly elected seats go to women. States decide Chairperson reservations and can reserve for backward classes, and SC and ST reservations end after the Article 334 period.

p: (1) Every Municipality, unless sooner dissolved under any law for the time being in force, shall continue for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer:
Provided that a Municipality shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before its dissolution.

(2) No amendment of any law for the time being in force shall have the effect of causing dissolution of a Municipality at any level, which is functioning immediately before such amendment, till the expiration of its duration specified in clause (1).
(3) An election to constitute a Municipality shall be completed,—
(a) before the expiry of its duration specified in clause (1);
(b) before the expiration of a period of six months from the date of its dissolution:

Provided that where the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Municipality would have continued is less than six months, it shall not be necessary to hold any election under this clause for constituting the Municipality for such period.

(4) A Municipality constituted upon the dissolution of a Municipality before the expiration of its duration shall continue only for the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Municipality would have continued under clause (1) had it not been so dissolved.
243U.s: A Municipality serves five years from its first meeting unless dissolved earlier after a reasonable hearing, and a change in law cannot cut a sitting Municipality's term short. Elections must finish before the term ends or within six months of dissolution, unless under six months remain, and a replacement body serves only the remaining term.

p: (1) A person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of a Municipality—
(a) if he is so disqualified by or under any law for the time being in force for the purposes of elections to the Legislature of the State concerned:
Provided that no person shall be disqualified on the ground that he is less than twenty-five years of age, if he has attained the age of twenty-one years;
(b) if he is so disqualified by or under any law made by the Legislature of the State.

(2) If any question arises as to whether a member of a Municipality has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1), the question shall be referred for the decision of such authority and in such manner as the Legislature of a State may, by law, provide.
243V.s: A person cannot be or become a Municipality member if disqualified under laws for State Legislature elections or any State law, though nobody aged 21 or more is disqualified for being under 25. The State Legislature sets who decides disqualification questions.

p: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the Legislature of a State may, by law, endow—

(a) the Municipalities with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as institutions of self-government and such law may contain provisions for the devolution of powers and responsibilities upon Municipalities, subject to such conditions as may be specified therein, with respect to—
(i) the preparation of plans for economic development and social justice;
(ii) the performance of functions and the implementation of schemes as may be entrusted to them including those in relation to the matters listed in the Twelfth Schedule;

(b) the Committees with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to carry out the responsibilities conferred upon them including those in relation to the matters listed in the Twelfth Schedule.
243W.s: The State Legislature can, by law, give Municipalities the powers they need as institutions of self-government, including preparing plans for economic development and social justice and carrying out schemes on Twelfth Schedule matters. It can also empower committees to do their duties.

p: The Legislature of a State may, by law,—
(a) authorise a Municipality to levy, collect and appropriate such taxes, duties, tolls and fees in accordance with such procedure and subject to such limits;
(b) assign to a Municipality such taxes, duties, tolls and fees levied and collected by the State Government for such purposes and subject to such conditions and limits;
(c) provide for making such grants-in-aid to the Municipalities from the Consolidated Fund of the State; and
(d) provide for constitution of such Funds for crediting all moneys received, respectively, by or on behalf of the Municipalities and also for the withdrawal of such moneys therefrom,
as may be specified in the law.
243X.s: The State Legislature can, by law, let Municipalities levy and collect taxes, duties, tolls and fees, hand them taxes collected by the State, give them grants from the State's Consolidated Fund, and set up funds to hold and pay out their money.

p: (1) The Finance Commission constituted under article 243I shall also review the financial position of the Municipalities and make recommendations to the Governor as to—
(a) the principles which should govern—

(i) the distribution between the State and the Municipalities of the net proceeds of the taxes, duties, tolls and fees leviable by the State, which may be divided between them under this Part and the allocation between the Municipalities at all levels of their respective shares of such proceeds;
(ii) the determination of the taxes, duties, tolls and fees which may be assigned to, or appropriated by, the Municipalities;
(iii) the grants-in-aid to the Municipalities from the Consolidated Fund of the State;
(b) the measures needed to improve the financial position of the Municipalities;
(c) any other matter referred to the Finance Commission by the Governor in the interests of sound finance of the Municipalities.

(2) The Governor shall cause every recommendation made by the Commission under this article together with an explanatory memorandum as to the action taken thereon to be laid before the Legislature of the State.
243Y.s: The State Finance Commission under Article 243I also reviews Municipalities' finances and recommends to the Governor how State taxes and fees are shared with them, which taxes they get, what grants they receive and how to improve their finances. The Governor places its recommendations and an action-taken note before the State Legislature.

p: The Legislature of a State may, by law, make provisions with respect to the maintenance of accounts by the Municipalities and the auditing of such accounts.
243Z.s: The State Legislature can make laws on how Municipalities keep their accounts and how those accounts are audited.

p: (1) The superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to the Municipalities shall be vested in the State Election Commission referred to in article 243K.

(2) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the Legislature of a State may, by law, make provision with respect to all matters relating to, or in connection with, elections to the Municipalities.
243ZA.s: The State Election Commission oversees and controls the preparation of voter lists and the conduct of all Municipality elections. The State Legislature can make laws on any matter relating to these elections.

p: The provisions of this Part shall apply to the Union territories and shall, in their application to a Union territory, have effect as if the references to the Governor of a State were references to the Administrator of the Union territory appointed under article 239 and references to the Legislature or the Legislative Assembly of a State were references in relation to a Union territory having a Legislative Assembly, to that Legislative Assembly:

Provided that the President may, by public notification, direct that the provisions of this Part shall apply to any Union territory or part thereof subject to such exceptions and modifications as he may specify in the notification.
243ZB.s: The Municipalities Part applies to Union territories, with the Administrator replacing the Governor and any Union territory Legislative Assembly replacing the State Legislature. The President can, by public notification, apply it to any Union territory with exceptions and changes.

p: (1) Nothing in this Part shall apply to the Scheduled Areas referred to in clause (1), and the tribal areas referred to in clause (2) of article 244.

(2) Nothing in this Part shall be construed to affect the functions and powers of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council constituted under any law for the time being in force for the hill areas of the district of Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal.

(3) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may, by law, extend the provisions of this Part to the Scheduled Areas and the tribal areas referred to in clause (1) subject to such exceptions and modifications as may be specified in such law, and no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.
243ZC.s: The Municipalities Part does not apply to Scheduled Areas and tribal areas under Article 244, and it does not affect the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council's powers. Parliament can extend it to those areas by law, with exceptions, and such a law does not count as a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
k: where municipality rules do not apply

p: (1) There shall be constituted in every State at the district level a District Planning Committee to consolidate the plans prepared by the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the district and to prepare a draft development plan for the district as a whole.
(2) The Legislature of a State may, by law, make provision with respect to—
(a) the composition of the District Planning Committees;
(b) the manner in which the seats in such Committees shall be filled:

Provided that not less than four-fifths of the total number of members of such Committee shall be elected by, and from amongst, the elected members of the Panchayat at the district level and of the Municipalities in the district in proportion to the ratio between the population of the rural areas and of the urban areas in the district;
(c) the functions relating to district planning which may be assigned to such Committees;
(d) the manner in which the Chairpersons of such Committees shall be chosen.
(3) Every District Planning Committee shall, in preparing the draft development plan,—
(a) have regard to—

(i) matters of common interest between the Panchayats and the Municipalities including spatial planning, sharing of water and other physical and natural resources, the integrated development of infrastructure and environmental conservation;
(ii) the extent and type of available resources whether financial or otherwise;
(b) consult such institutions and organisations as the Governor may, by order, specify.
(4) The Chairperson of every District Planning Committee shall forward the development plan, as recommended by such Committee, to the Government of the State.
243ZD.s: Every State must set up District Planning Committees to combine Panchayat and Municipality plans into a draft development plan for each district, considering shared resources, and send it to the State Government. At least four-fifths of members are elected by and from elected local body members, in proportion to rural and urban population.

p: (1) There shall be constituted in every Metropolitan area a Metropolitan Planning Committee to prepare a draft development plan for the Metropolitan area as a whole.
(2) The Legislature of a State may, by law, make provision with respect to—
(a) the composition of the Metropolitan Planning Committees;
(b) the manner in which the seats in such Committees shall be filled:

Provided that not less than two-thirds of the members of such Committee shall be elected by, and from amongst, the elected members of the Municipalities and Chairpersons of the Panchayats in the Metropolitan area in proportion to the ratio between the population of the Municipalities and of the Panchayats in that area;

(c) the representation in such Committees of the Government of India and the Government of the State and of such organisations and institutions as may be deemed necessary for carrying out the functions assigned to such Committees;
(d) the functions relating to planning and coordination for the Metropolitan area which may be assigned to such Committees;
(e) the manner in which the Chairpersons of such Committees shall be chosen.
(3) Every Metropolitan Planning Committee shall, in preparing the draft development plan,—
(a) have regard to—
(i) the plans prepared by the Municipalities and the Panchayats in the Metropolitan area;

(ii) matters of common interest between the Municipalities and the Panchayats, including coordinated spatial planning of the area, sharing of water and other physical and natural resources, the integrated development of infrastructure and environmental conservation;
(iii) the overall objectives and priorities set by the Government of India and the Government of the State;

(iv) the extent and nature of investments likely to be made in the Metropolitan area by agencies of the Government of India and of the Government of the State and other available resources whether financial or otherwise;
(b) consult such institutions and organisations as the Governor may, by order, specify.
(4) The Chairperson of every Metropolitan Planning Committee shall forward the development plan, as recommended by such Committee, to the Government of the State.
243ZE.s: Every Metropolitan area must have a Metropolitan Planning Committee to prepare a draft development plan for the whole area, considering local plans, shared resources, government priorities and investment, and send it to the State Government. At least two-thirds of members are elected by and from elected Municipality members and Panchayat chairpersons, in proportion to their populations.

p: Notwithstanding anything in this Part, any provision of any law relating to Municipalities in force in a State immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventy-fourth Amendment) Act, 1992, which is inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall continue to be in force until amended or repealed by a competent Legislature or other competent authority or until the expiration of one year from such commencement, whichever is earlier:

Provided that all the Municipalities existing immediately before such commencement shall continue till the expiration of their duration, unless sooner dissolved by a resolution passed to that effect by the Legislative Assembly of that State or, in the case of a State having a Legislative Council, by each House of the Legislature of that State.
243ZF.s: A transitional rule from 1992: State Municipality laws that conflict with this Part stayed in force for at most one year after the Seventy-fourth Amendment unless changed sooner. Existing Municipalities could finish their terms unless dissolved earlier by a resolution of the State Legislature.

p: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,—

(a) the validity of any law relating to the delimitation of constituencies or the allotment of seats to such constituencies, made or purporting to be made under article 243ZA shall not be called in question in any court;

(b) no election to any Municipality shall be called in question except by an election petition presented to such authority and in such manner as is provided for by or under any law made by the Legislature of a State.]
243ZG.s: Courts cannot question laws on drawing Municipality constituencies or allotting seats to them. A Municipality election can be challenged only through an election petition, before the authority and in the way set by State law.

why: Minerva Mills (1980) held that setting aside Articles 14 and 19 for a whole class of laws destroys the basic structure; Coelho (2007) treats the core of Articles 14, 19 and 21 as the test for Ninth Schedule laws.
Coelho (2007) called Article 32 "an important and integral part of the basic structure", and L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that judicial review under it cannot be ousted.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that the High Courts' power of judicial review under Article 226, and their superintendence under Article 227, are part of the inviolable basic structure.
Minerva Mills (1980) held that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature, so Parliament cannot amend this article to make its power unlimited.

The NJAC case (2015) struck down the Ninety-ninth Amendment's new method of appointing judges as a breach of judicial independence, so the core of how judges are appointed is part of the basic structure.
Names India as a Union of States. Abolishing the Union or the States would undo federalism and India's sovereignty, both part of the framework.
This is the hook for testing laws against fundamental rights. Courts have said the power to test legislation "can never be ousted".
Core guarantees against discrimination and untouchability. Coelho (2007) named Article 15 among the rights forming part of the basic structure.
Freedom of religion is the main textual home of secularism, which the Court has repeatedly called a basic feature.
Judicial review by the High Courts, held to be basic, depends on the High Courts existing.
Adult suffrage is the foundation of democracy and free and fair elections.

Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held that, apart from the part that relates to the basic structure, the Preamble does not limit the power to amend. Balram Singh (2024) rejected a challenge to adding "socialist" and "secular" in 1976.
Defines "the State" against which fundamental rights are enforced; gutting it would hollow out the rights.
Equality of opportunity in public employment is part of the equality code, though clauses on reservation have been changed and upheld.
Basic protections of personal liberty and fair criminal process, closely tied to Article 21.
Bans on forced labour and child labour in hazardous work relate to human dignity; no case has tested their repeal.
Religious freedom of groups and the bar on State religious instruction carry secularism into practice.
Minority rights to culture and to run educational institutions support pluralism and secularism.
The Directive to separate the judiciary from the executive expresses separation of powers and judicial independence.
An elected President as head of state is part of the republican form of government.
How the President is elected. Entrenched: changing it needs ratification by half the States.
Extent of Union executive power, one half of the federal balance. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
Ministers advise the President and answer collectively to the Lok Sabha: the core of parliamentary government.
An elected Parliament, with the States represented in it. Representation of the States is entrenched.
Fixed terms for the Houses guarantee periodic elections.
Parliament cannot discuss a judge's conduct except on a motion for removal, a rule tied to judicial independence.
Judges' salaries cannot be cut to their disadvantage while in office, a guard on judicial independence.
Courts of record with power to punish contempt, part of the courts' ability to make their orders effective.
The Supreme Court settles disputes between the Union and the States, a federal safeguard.
Special leave to appeal lets the Supreme Court correct any court or tribunal, central to access to justice.
Each State has its own executive, part of the federal structure.
Extent of State executive power. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
State ministers advise the Governor and answer to the Assembly: parliamentary government at State level.
An elected State Legislature with fixed terms, needed for both democracy and federalism.
Transfers of High Court judges. The NJAC case struck down the 2014 change to this article as part of the same scheme.
High Court control over the subordinate courts keeps the district judiciary independent of the executive.
The division of law-making power between Parliament and the States. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
No tax without the authority of law, a basic rule-of-law guarantee.
An independent Election Commission conducts elections; without it free and fair elections would be at risk.
A single electoral roll with no exclusion on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
The right to education. Its insertion was upheld, but no case says whether removing it would breach the basic structure.
The welfare-state directives most closely tied to the balance between Parts III and IV. Removing them might upset that balance; untested.
Courts cannot question the validity of legislative proceedings on grounds of procedure. Touches both separation of powers and judicial review.
Binding precedent and the power to do complete justice. Important to the Court's role, but not tested as basic.
An independent auditor of public accounts supports the rule of law and accountability; untested.
Organisational rules for the High Courts. Some core is needed for judicial review, but the details can change.
President's Rule. Its use is reviewable (Bommai), and abuse can damage federalism and democracy, but the article itself is not part of the basic structure.
Suspension of rights during emergency. Since 1978, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended; widening this power again could touch the core of rights.
Parliament already changes State boundaries by ordinary law; the federal structure survives individual changes.
Citizenship rules. Parliament already controls citizenship by law under Article 11.
These shield certain laws from fundamental rights challenges. Removing them would restore rights, not damage the structure.
Powers to adapt or restrict rights for armed forces and martial law; administrative in nature.
Individual Directive Principles. The balance between Parts III and IV is basic, but no single directive has been held essential.
Fundamental duties were added in 1976 and are not enforceable in court.
Detailed rules on the President, Vice-President and conduct of business. Can change without touching a basic feature.
Detailed rules on Parliament's membership, officers and procedure.
Legislative and financial procedure, and ordinances. Can be redesigned without damaging democracy itself.
Organisation and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court beyond its core review power. Many have been amended before.
Form and reporting of public accounts.
Detailed rules on Governors and State executive business.
Detailed rules on State Legislatures, their officers and members.
State legislative and financial procedure, assent to Bills and ordinances.
Detailed rules on High Court judges and jurisdiction beyond the core review power.
Appointment and rules for district judges and subordinate courts.
How Union territories are governed. Parliament has changed this often.
Panchayats, added in 1992. Local democracy, but not part of the original framework or any holding.
Administration of Scheduled and Tribal Areas.
Specific rules within the division of legislative power. Entrenched where in Chapter I of Part XI, but individually changeable.
Administrative relations between the Union and the States.
Distribution of revenues and the Finance Commission. Revised many times, including by GST in 2016.
Freedom of trade within India and its exceptions.
Civil services and Public Service Commissions.
Tribunals may exist; what is part of the basic structure is the High Courts' and Supreme Court's review over them, not these articles.
Election law-making and the bar on courts during elections.
Reservations in legislatures and services, commissions and lists. Many have sunset clauses or have been amended; upheld when changed.
Linguistic minority protections and the Hindi directive.
Emergency powers. The articles themselves are not part of the basic structure.
Transitional provisions continuing earlier laws, courts and officers.
The right to property. Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held it is not part of the basic structure.
Temporary and special provisions for particular States. Several have been changed or ended, and the changes upheld.
Abolition of titles. An equality measure, but minor; no case suggests it is essential.
Equal justice and free legal aid, the directive most closely tied to effective access to justice.
Concurrent power over GST, added in 2016. A specific fiscal arrangement within federalism.
Interpretation clause for the Part on finance.
Co-operative societies, added in 2011. Detailed regulatory rules.
Salaries of members and rules of procedure and language in Parliament.
Definitions, interpretation, short title, commencement, the Hindi text and repeals.
Lists the States and Union territories. Parliament changes it by ordinary law under Articles 3 and 4.
Salaries and allowances of constitutional office-holders.
Forms of oaths, including the oath to uphold the Constitution.
Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats. Entrenched, but the numbers change by amendment.
Autonomous districts in the North-East; amended many times.
The Union, State and Concurrent Lists as a scheme are the core of federalism. Individual entries are changed often.
Laws shielded from fundamental rights challenges. Removing the shield would not damage the structure.
The anti-defection law, upheld in Kihoto Hollohan. Repealing it would not breach a basic feature.

democracy.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
democracy.s: Government by elected representatives, with an elected head of state.

q.t: Democracy and federalism are the essential features of our Constitution and are part of its basic structure.
q.by: Sawant J, for Kuldip Singh J and himself

secular.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994); I.R. Coelho (2007); Balram Singh (2024)
secular.s: The State treats all religions equally and has no religion of its own.

q.t: Secularism is one of the basic features of the Constitution. While freedom of religion is guaranteed to all persons in India, from the point of view of the State, the religion, faith or belief of a person is immaterial.
q.by: Jeevan Reddy J, for S.C. Agrawal J and himself

federal.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
federal.s: Power is divided between the Union and the States, and the States are not mere agents of the Centre.

q.t: The above discussion thus shows that the States have an independent constitutional existence and they have as important a role to play in the political, social, educational and cultural life of the people as the Union. They are neither satellites nor agents of the Centre.
q.by: Sawant J, for Kuldip Singh J and himself

sop.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); I.R. Coelho (2007)
sop.s: Legislature, executive and judiciary each keep their own sphere.

q.t: Equality, rule of law, judicial review and separation of powers form parts of the basic structure of the Constitution. ... All these would be redundant if the legislative, executive and judicial powers are vested in one organ.
q.by: Sabharwal CJ, for the nine-judge bench

sb.case: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn v Union of India (2015)

rol.c: P. Sambamurthy (1986); I.R. Coelho (2007); Raj Narain (1975)
rol.s: Government acts under law, and its decisions can be tested by independent courts.

q.t: ...the rule of law which is clearly a basic and essential feature of the Constitution. It is a basic principle of the rule of law that the exercise of power by the executive or any other authority must not only be conditioned by the Constitution but must also be in accordance with law...

sb.what: Art. 371D(5) and the condition attached to it (State Government could modify or annul tribunal orders)
sb.case: P. Sambamurthy v State of Andhra Pradesh (1986)

equality.t: Equality and the core of fundamental rights
equality.s: The core of Articles 14, 19 and 21, and of each fundamental right, cannot be taken away.

q.t: India's constitutional history has led us to include the essence of each of our fundamental rights in the basic structure of our Constitution.
q.by: Sabharwal CJ, for the nine-judge bench

balance.t: Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
balance.s: Parts III and IV must be kept in harmony; neither may be made to swallow the other.

q.t: To give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution. This harmony and balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution.

sb.what: 42nd Amendment s.4 widening Art. 31C to ‘all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV’
sb.case: Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980)

jr.s: The High Courts and the Supreme Court must be able to test laws and government action against the Constitution.

q.t: We, therefore, hold that the power of judicial review over legislative action vested in the High Courts under Articles 226 and in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution is an integral and essential feature of the Constitution, constituting part of its basic structure.
q.by: Ahmadi CJ, for the seven-judge bench

sb.what: Art. 323A(2)(d) and 323B(3)(d), to the extent they exclude Arts. 226/227 and 32
sb.case: L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India (1997)

indep.s: Judges must be appointed, and do their work, free of control by the executive.

q.t: The expectation from the judiciary, to safeguard the rights of the citizens of this country, can only be ensured, by keeping it absolutely insulated and independent, from the other organs of governance.

sb.case: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn v Union of India (2015)

access.s: People must be able to reach a court to enforce their rights. The right to go to the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself part of the basic structure.

q.t: The existence of the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution at will, with requisite voting strength, so as to make any kind of laws that excludes Part III including power of judicial review under Article 32 is incompatible with the basic structure doctrine.
q.by: Sabharwal CJ, for the nine-judge bench

amend.s: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but cannot use that power to destroy its identity or make the power unlimited.

q.t: Indeed, a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution and therefore, the limitations on that power cannot be destroyed.

sb.what: Art. 368(4) and (5), inserted by 42nd Amendment s.55
sb.case: Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980)

sovereign.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973; Shelat and Grover JJ, Hegde and Mukherjea JJ)
sovereign.s: India is a sovereign Union; its unity and integrity are part of the framework.

at.KB: pp. 280-281 (Shelat and Grover JJ) and p. 322 (Hegde and Mukherjea JJ)

q.t: ... the Parliament has no power to abrogate or emasculate the basic elements or fundamental features of the Constitution such as the sovereignty of India, the democratic character of our polity, the unity of the country, ...

parl.s: Ministers are drawn from and answerable to an elected legislature.

q.t: A sovereign democratic republic, Parliamentary democracy, the three organs of the State, certainly in my view constitute the basic structure.

elections.c: Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975, Khanna J)
elections.s: Elections must be free and fair, and their results open to lawful challenge.

q.t: ...I strike down clause (4) of article 329A on the ground that it violates the principle of free and fair elections which is an essential postulate of democracy and which in its turn is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution...

supremacy.s: Every organ of the State is bound by the Constitution.

q.t: The true position is that every provision of the Constitution can be amended provided in the result the basic foundation and structure of the constitution remains the same. The basic structure may be said to consist of the following features : (1) Supremacy of the Constitution; ...
